description: We were motivated and excited about space, mission, exploration and always wanted to join NASA, But eventually the dream started vanishing because we thought it would simply be impossible. So, I started to ignore the dream. As a result, we almost forget our dream. But after seeing the NASA Space Apps challenge, we were motivated and excited again to try one more time. So, we decided to built an impactful website which aligned with this challenge.
summary:
An interactive 3D website to learn easily and smoothly. Landing Safety Zones: establish safety zones on the Moon and Mars for preserving previous landing sites, allowing users to log in, plan launches, and check if proposed landing locations for rovers or machinery are safe.
Earth's Scars and Climate Change: Earth observation, tracking surface activities and environmental changes over the past century such as the drying of the Caspian Sea and the Aral Sea, and the impacts of global warming.
COSMIC RELICS & RESTING SITES: tracking ongoing and past human missions in deep space, from the beginning of history up to current programs like Artemis and Apollo etc.
details:
Summary

Planetary Footprint is an interactive 3D website that makes space exploration and Earth’s changing environment easy to learn. It connects three ideas: the permanent hardware humanity has left in space, the scars we have left on Earth, and the responsibility to protect both. It has three sections:

  1. 3D Telemetry. A live WebGL view of the solar system built on NASA Eyes. Users can follow spacecraft such as Voyager 1, Perseverance, Dawn, Pioneer 10 and Kepler, as well as the Moon, Mars and the Earth fleet. They can also inspect 3D hardware models such as the Apollo Lunar Module, Cassini-Huygens, a Deep Space Network dish and asteroid Bennu.
  2. Cosmic Relics & Landing Simulator. A catalog of 13 relics from the NSSDCA master catalog, from early missions to current programs like Artemis. A 3D simulator lets users test how a lander’s rocket plume would affect protected sites on the Moon and Mars.
  3. Earth Scars Observatory. A before-and-now satellite comparison tool for the Aral Sea, the Caspian Sea, Arctic ice and glaciers. It shows how warming and human activity have reshaped the planet over the past century.

What does it do and how does it work?

  • Learning by exploring. Users drag to orbit, scroll to zoom and click through missions. Positions come from NASA’s JPL SPICE ephemeris through NASA Eyes, so they are real rather than illustrative.
  • Landing Safety Zones. The relics page marks protected zones around historic landing sites, such as the six Apollo descent stages that remain on the Moon. Users can log in, plan a launch, and propose a landing location for a rover or machinery. The system checks the proposed site against a safety buffer (for example, an 80 km plume buffer in the Artemis section). It then reports whether the site is safe or would endanger a heritage site.
  • Earth observation. Side-by-side satellite imagery from NASA Earth Observatory lets users compare the same place across time and see environmental change directly.

What benefits does it have?

  • Complex space and climate data becomes visual and hands-on, so students and the general public can learn without technical knowledge.
  • It brings space history, planetary protection and climate science into one smooth experience, instead of scattering them across separate sites.
  • It uses trusted sources (NASA, NSSDCA, JPL) in a form that runs in any browser without installation.
  • Its safety-check concept gives mission planners and learners a simple way to see how a landing could damage existing sites.

What is the intended impact?

  • Education. Make learning about space and climate engaging for students and curious visitors.
  • Preservation. Raise awareness that human landing sites are cultural and scientific heritage. The Moon and Mars should not repeat the careless pattern we left on Earth.
  • Climate awareness. Show clearly, with real satellite evidence, how the Aral Sea, the Caspian Sea, Arctic ice and glaciers have changed.
  • Responsible exploration. Encourage a shared habit of planning missions with preservation in mind, from Apollo-era sites to Artemis.

What tools, languages, hardware or software did you use?

  • Data and imagery: NASA Eyes on the Solar System (WebGL, JPL SPICE ephemeris), NASA 3D Resources models, the NSSDCA master catalog, NASA Earth Observatory satellite imagery.
  • Front end: HTML, CSS and JavaScript, with WebGL for the 3D views.
  • Hosting and development: Deployed on Vercel.
  • Hardware: Runs in any modern browser on a laptop, desktop or mobile device. No special hardware is needed.

How is your project creative?

  • It treats space heritage and Earth’s climate damage as one story: the footprints we leave on other worlds mirror the scars we have left at home.
  • It moves from passive viewing to interactive decision-making: instead of only looking at sites, users test whether a landing would be safe.
  • It uses a mission-control “telemetry console” look, with a live UTC clock, Voyager 1’s distance in AU and relic counters, to make learning feel like operating a real mission.
  • It combines a live NASA 3D view, a hardware model lab, a plume simulator and a satellite comparison tool in one smooth, linked experience.

What factors did your team consider?

  • Accuracy. Everything is based on NASA and NSSDCA sources and real ephemeris data.
  • Accessibility and simplicity. The interface is easy to use, needs no installation and works across devices.
  • Performance. Heavy 3D content is meant to load smoothly in the browser.
  • Scientific meaning. The safety buffer should reflect real concerns, namely that lander plumes can throw debris and damage nearby historic hardware.
  • Ethics and preservation. Protecting the first human footprints on other worlds matters as much as exploring new ones.
  • Scalability. More relics, planets and Earth-change locations can be added over time.
